name: Checkout Platform — Distributed Transaction & Event Architecture Review
notes: Lines are source lines of the sample file. 'categories' lists every category the item may correctly appear as; the first is its main one (used for per-category recall). optional items are fine to extract but not counted as missed.

items.text: Publish events through an outbox table in PostgreSQL, the single write path, with independent publishers
Payment authorization stays synchronous; do not make it asynchronous until failure semantics are validated
Default Kafka partition key is order_id; consumers needing stronger ordering solve it in their own domain
Do not impose customer-level partitioning on the whole platform
Explicit topic-level ACL permissions for producers and consumers are mandatory for production; no shared service account
Short-lived workload credentials preferred over static secrets, not a hard launch blocker
Read replicas not used for transactional reads or payment status; maybe operational queries after measuring replica lag
Standardize retry policies with exponential backoff, at least for infrastructure events
Dead-letter handling after the retry policy is exhausted
Checkout API should not wait for Kafka consumer processing; separate user-facing completion from background retries
No sensitive payment information in event payloads or application logs
Encryption in transit is mandatory
At-rest encryption verified and documented as infrastructure configuration, not assumed from the provider
Security review is a production gate covering ACLs, credential lifecycle, event payloads and threat modeling
Event IDs generated once in the transactional boundary, stored in the outbox record and reused by every publisher
At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers; exactly-once is not required
Every migrated consumer needs idempotency based on event ID
PostgreSQL remains the durable idempotency source for payment-related processing
Event schemas need compatibility rules: backward compatibility at minimum, breaking changes require a new event version
Consumers should not silently accept unknown fields
Contract tests for event schemas
A schema registry is part of the migration
OpenTelemetry tracing across Kafka; trace IDs propagate through message headers
Metrics include consumer lag, retry counts, dead-letter volume, processing latency and outbox publishing latency
No universal consumer lag alert threshold; thresholds are topic-specific
Canary migration with a rollback mechanism before exposing production traffic
Rollback triggers: elevated error rate, consumer lag, duplicate processing, database saturation; payment failures get their own threshold
Define actual rollback thresholds before the first production canary
Do not choose Kafka retention until legal and compliance confirm the requirement
No production schema change until the database benchmark is reviewed; benchmark is a gate before production rollout
Schema design can proceed before the benchmark; final production configuration not locked until database overhead is known
Idempotency record and payment state committed atomically in the same database transaction
New checkout path available before the November promotion
Own the outbox schema and transaction-state changes
Own Kafka infrastructure, ACLs, observability and migration tooling
Benchmark PostgreSQL indexing, outbox overhead and Redis versus PostgreSQL deduplication
Document payment idempotency and fraud ordering requirements
Own the threat model and security review
Define the event contracts and migration architecture
Coordinate the rollout schedule and campaign deadline
Database commit and message publication are not atomic: events lost after commit, or orders seen that rolled back
Outbox insert on every transaction adds database load; database strains near 11,000 writes per minute with connection pool saturation
Authorization response can arrive after a timeout; an API timeout does not mean the payment failed
A client retrying the checkout endpoint could create two authorization attempts
Kafka ordering only within a partition; consumer semantics differ from RabbitMQ
Fraud scoring may need customer-level ordering that order_id partitioning does not give
Customer-level partitioning creates hot keys for enterprise customers; changing the partition key later is not trivial
Identity integration for short-lived credentials may not be ready in time
Reconciliation query every minute could become expensive and may need a composite or partial index
Read replica lag gives stale data, unacceptable for payment status
Services retry inconsistently: three times, five times, payment integration its own way
Without a maximum retry window an event can keep retrying for hours
A retry can keep the checkout workflow alive after the user has timed out
Dual publishing can publish one message and fail the other
During migration duplicate events may be published into two systems
If Redis loses state an event may be processed again
Durable PostgreSQL deduplication adds an extra database lookup that increases database load
Five weeks to the November promotion is aggressive for changing infrastructure and migrating consumers
What is the maximum retry window? Fifteen minutes was only an example
Will Redis deduplication stay? Undecided; benchmark without Redis first
Which schema registry: Confluent Schema Registry or the cloud provider's native registry
Topic-specific consumer lag alert thresholds remain to be defined
Actual rollback thresholds for the production canary
Initial canary traffic percentage, 1% or 5%
How long to keep Kafka transaction events; retention pending legal and compliance
Exact threat-model scope still needs to be finalized
Whether the reconciliation query needs a composite or partial index, pending benchmark
